ambiguities.text: Execution layer clients have different configuration formats. They should all update the gas limit value generated in their default configurations to 60M.
ambiguities.resolution_strategy: Assume 'default configurations' means the value used when no operator override is specified. Operators who have manually set a gas limit will retain their custom value. This is an assumption that should be verified per-client.

ambiguities.text: The EIP does not specify whether the gas limit change takes effect at a specific block number, at the Fusaka fork boundary, or is simply a client default that validators vote on.
ambiguities.resolution_strategy: Assume this is a soft default change: clients ship with 60M as the default, and validators organically adopt it via the gas limit voting mechanism. This means actual on-chain gas limit may take time to reach 60M after Fusaka deployment.

ambiguities.text: Coordination with transaction-level gas limit proposals may be necessary, as higher block limits could enable transactions exceeding separate transaction gas constraints.
ambiguities.resolution_strategy: Assume there may be a separate per-transaction gas limit proposal (not yet finalized) that would cap individual transaction gas. Without such a cap, a single transaction could theoretically consume the entire 60M gas block. Treat this as an open coordination risk.

implicit_assumptions.description: All major EL client implementations will update their default gas limit in a coordinated manner at or before Fusaka activation.
implicit_assumptions.impact_if_false: If some clients default to 36M and others to 60M, validators running different clients would produce blocks with different gas limits, causing temporary inconsistency in network capacity and potential MEV imbalances.

implicit_assumptions.description: Node hardware can handle the increased computational and storage demands of 60M gas blocks (approximately 67% increase over 36M).
implicit_assumptions.impact_if_false: Nodes with insufficient resources may fall behind in block processing, leading to increased uncle rates, longer sync times, and potential centralization pressure toward more powerful hardware.

implicit_assumptions.description: Adversarial block constructions that maximize worst-case block size are already researched and do not pose a threat below 150M gas.
implicit_assumptions.impact_if_false: If novel adversarial constructions exist that increase worst-case block size beyond current estimates at 60M gas, blocks could approach or exceed the 10 MiB CL gossip limit, disrupting block propagation and potentially causing missed slots.

implicit_assumptions.description: The existing gas limit voting mechanism will smoothly transition the network gas limit from 36M to 60M after client defaults are updated.
implicit_assumptions.impact_if_false: If a significant fraction of validators do not update or override defaults, the gas limit may not reach 60M, or the transition may be slow and unpredictable, creating uncertainty for users and applications.

implicit_assumptions.description: Existing smart contracts deployed on mainnet will continue to function correctly under 60M gas blocks.
implicit_assumptions.impact_if_false: Contracts that rely on assumptions about block gas limits (e.g., for gas estimation or reentrancy guards based on gas availability) could behave unexpectedly, potentially enabling exploits.
